questions.question: What is the sliding window technique and when do you use it?
questions.title: Sliding Window Technique Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Sliding window** maintains a window (subarray or substring) that slides over the data. Instead of recomputing from scratch, you add the new element entering the window and remove the element leaving. Turns O(n²) solutions into O(n) for contiguous subarray problems.

interviewer_intent.testing: Pattern recognition for contiguous subarray/substring problems
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Recomputing the sum from scratch for each window position — O(n²) instead of O(n)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the two types: fixed-size window and variable-size window — they have slightly different implementation patterns

sections.title: Add Right, Remove Left — O(n)
sections.content: **Fixed-size window**: window of size k slides one step at a time. Add `arr[right]` to window, remove `arr[left]` when window size exceeds k. Classic: maximum sum subarray of size k. **Variable-size window**: expand right when condition not met, shrink left when condition violated. Classic: longest substring without repeating characters. The key insight: each element is added once and removed once — **total O(n)** regardless of window movement.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Fixed window: right - left + 1 == k → shrink by moving left
- Variable window: expand right freely, shrink left when invalid
- Each element enters and exits window at most once → O(n)
- Fixed: max sum, average, product of k elements
- Variable: longest substring no repeat, smallest subarray sum >= k
- Track window state with sum, HashMap, or frequency array
- Right pointer always advances; left advances only when needed

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The sliding window technique avoids recomputing the window from scratch at each position. Instead, as the window slides one step, I add the new right element and remove the old left element. For a fixed-size window, I subtract the outgoing element and add the incoming one — O(1) per step. For a variable-size window like longest substring without repeating characters, I expand right as long as valid and shrink left when I hit a violation. Since each element is added and removed at most once, the total is O(n). I identify this pattern when the problem asks for something optimal about a contiguous subarray or substring.

questions.question: How do you find the maximum sum subarray of size k?
questions.title: Maximum Sum Subarray Size K Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Compute the sum of the first k elements, then slide the window: add the next element and subtract the element leaving the window.** Track the maximum sum seen. O(n) time, O(1) space — far better than O(n²) with nested loops.

interviewer_intent.testing: Classic fixed-size sliding window — the entry point for the pattern
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a nested loop to recompute the sum for each window — O(n²)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Code it cleanly and explain the slide operation: maxSum = Math.max(maxSum, windowSum)

sections.title: Fixed Window: Slide and Track Maximum
sections.content: Phase 1: compute `windowSum` for the first k elements. Phase 2: slide from index k to n-1: `windowSum += arr[i] - arr[i-k]` (add incoming, remove outgoing). Update `maxSum = Math.max(maxSum, windowSum)`. This works because consecutive windows differ by exactly one element on each end — no need to sum from scratch. Edge case: if k > array length, return -1 or throw exception.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Phase 1: sum first k elements — O(k)
- Phase 2: slide n-k times, each O(1) → O(n)
- Slide operation: windowSum += arr[i] - arr[i-k]
- Track maxSum = Math.max(maxSum, windowSum)
- Time: O(n), Space: O(1)
- Extension: max average subarray of size k (divide by k at end)
- Brute force: O(n*k) — two loops, computing fresh sum each time

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: First I compute the sum of the initial window of size k. Then I slide the window across the array: at each step I add the new right element and subtract the element that just left the left side. I track the maximum sum seen at any window position. This is O(n) because I never sum more than one element per step after the initialization. I'd contrast this with the naive approach of summing k elements for each of the n windows, which is O(n times k). The sliding window avoids the redundant computation.

questions.question: How do you find the longest substring without repeating characters?
questions.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Use a variable sliding window with a HashSet.** Expand the right pointer, adding characters to the set. When a duplicate is found, shrink from the left until the duplicate is removed. Track the maximum window size. O(n) time, O(min(n,m)) space where m = alphabet size.

interviewer_intent.testing: Variable-size sliding window with character tracking — the most classic sliding window interview problem
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a nested loop to check each substring for duplicates — O(n²) or O(n³)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use a HashMap that stores the character's most recent index for O(1) left-pointer jump instead of shrinking one step at a time

sections.title: Variable Window with HashSet or HashMap
sections.content: **HashSet approach**: `left = 0`, scan right. If `s.charAt(right)` is already in set — remove `s.charAt(left)` and `left++` until removed. Add current char and update `maxLen = right - left + 1`. **HashMap optimization**: store char → last seen index. When duplicate found at position `right`, jump `left = Math.max(left, map.get(c) + 1)` directly — no need to shrink one step at a time. Both O(n) but HashMap avoids redundant shrinking.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- HashSet approach: O(n) but may shrink one step at a time
- HashMap approach: O(n), jump left directly to skip repeated chars
- left = Math.max(left, map.get(c) + 1) — don't go backwards
- maxLen = Math.max(maxLen, right - left + 1)
- Time: O(n), Space: O(min(n, m)) — m = charset size
- Each character: at most one add and one remove from set
- Common variant: longest substring with at most k distinct characters

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I use a variable sliding window with a HashMap that maps each character to its most recent index. I expand the right pointer through the string. When I encounter a character already in the map, I jump the left pointer directly to one past where that character was last seen — rather than shrinking one step at a time. I use Math.max to avoid moving left backwards. At each step I update the maximum window size. This is O(n) because the right pointer only moves forward, and the left pointer can only move right. I'd mention the HashSet alternative if the interviewer wants a simpler version.

questions.question: How do you find all anagrams of a pattern in a string?
questions.title: Find All Anagrams in String Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Use a fixed-size sliding window of size p.length() with frequency arrays.** Maintain character counts for the window and pattern. When counts match, an anagram exists at the current window start. O(n) time using array comparison.

interviewer_intent.testing: Combining fixed-size sliding window with the frequency counting pattern
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Sorting each window substring to check anagram — O(n*k*log k) instead of O(n)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use Arrays.equals() on two int[26] arrays for O(26) = O(1) comparison, and explain the update logic clearly

sections.title: Fixed Window + Frequency Array Comparison
sections.content: Maintain `pCount[26]` for the pattern and `wCount[26]` for the current window. Initialize both for the first window of size p.length(). Then slide: add `s.charAt(right)` to wCount, remove `s.charAt(right - p.length())`. Compare `Arrays.equals(pCount, wCount)` — O(26) = O(1). If equal, add `right - p.length() + 1` to results. Total: **O(n)** overall.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Window size: fixed at p.length()
- Two int[26] arrays: pattern count and window count
- Arrays.equals(pCount, wCount): O(26) = O(1) comparison
- Slide: add incoming char, remove outgoing char
- Collect start indices of all matching windows
- Time: O(n), Space: O(1) — fixed 26-char arrays
- Alternative: use a 'match count' variable to avoid array comparison each step

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I use a fixed-size sliding window equal to the pattern length with two character frequency arrays of size 26. I initialize both with the pattern and the first window. Then I slide across the string: add the incoming right character and remove the outgoing left character from the window count. After each slide I compare the two arrays — since they're both size 26, that comparison is O(1). When they match I add the window start index to my result. Total time is O(n) and space is O(1) since the arrays are fixed size. A more optimized version avoids the array comparison by tracking how many characters currently match.

questions.question: How do you find the longest substring with at most K distinct characters?
questions.title: Longest Substring with At Most K Distinct Characters
questions.direct_answer: Use a variable-size sliding window with a HashMap tracking character frequencies; expand right freely and shrink from the left whenever the number of distinct characters exceeds K.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can adapt the sliding window template to a constraint involving distinct character counts
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting to remove the key from the map when its count drops to zero, causing incorrect distinct-character counts
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Call out the map-key-removal edge case explicitly and state the time complexity as O(n)

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
I use a variable-size sliding window combined with a HashMap. The HashMap stores each character as a key and its frequency within the current window as the value. The number of keys in the map equals the number of distinct characters in the window.

I maintain a left and right pointer, both starting at 0. I advance the right pointer, add the character at right to the map (increment its count), then check: if the map now has more than K keys, I shrink the window from the left. I decrement the count of the character at left; if that count reaches zero I remove the key from the map — this is a critical step that beginners often miss. I then increment left. I continue shrinking until the map has at most K keys.

After each valid window state I update maxLength as right - left + 1.

The time complexity is O(n) because each character is added and removed at most once. Space is O(K) for the map.

I also mention the edge case where K is zero or the string is empty, which should return zero.

sections.title: Key Points
content: HashMap: key=character, value=frequency in window; map.size() = distinct char count
Expand right; when map.size() > K, shrink from left
Remove map key when its count reaches 0 — critical to keep distinct count accurate
maxLength = max(maxLength, right - left + 1) after each valid window

questions.question: What is the difference between a fixed-size and variable-size sliding window?
questions.title: Fixed-Size vs Variable-Size Sliding Window
questions.direct_answer: A fixed window maintains a constant size by always removing the leftmost element before adding a new right element, while a variable window expands until a condition is violated then shrinks from the left until valid again.

interviewer_intent.testing: Conceptual clarity on the two sliding window variants and ability to pick the right one
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Applying a fixed-size template to a variable-size problem and getting wrong answers
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one concrete example for each variant and state the problem property that tells you which to use

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
There are two variants of the sliding window pattern and choosing the wrong one for a problem is a common mistake.

A fixed-size window always has exactly K elements. When you move the window one step right, you simultaneously remove the leftmost element and add the new rightmost element. The window size never changes. A classic example is finding the maximum sum of any K consecutive elements — you add the new element, subtract the element that fell off the left, and check if the current sum beats the maximum.

A variable-size window expands and contracts based on a condition. You advance the right pointer freely, adding elements to the window. When the window violates a constraint — such as the sum exceeding a target, or too many distinct characters — you shrink from the left until the window is valid again. You track the best (largest or smallest) valid window you have seen. An example is finding the smallest subarray with a sum greater than or equal to a target.

The signal in the problem tells you which to use: if the problem specifies a fixed K, use the fixed variant. If the problem asks for the longest or shortest subarray satisfying a condition without fixing the size, use the variable variant.

Both run in O(n) time because each element enters and exits the window at most once.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Fixed: window size = constant K; add rightmost, remove leftmost simultaneously
Variable: expand right freely; shrink left when constraint violated
Fixed example: max sum of K elements
Variable example: smallest subarray with sum >= target, longest substring with K distinct chars
Both are O(n) — each element enters and exits at most once
